newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen easing at opening.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen easing at opening.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open on the downside on Friday as investors seek to find their footing after Thursday's thrashing of technology stocks.
But traders will be looking at revised fourth quarter gross domestic product data, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, which could provide support for stocks if bonds reacted favorably.
"The big catch today is what happens in the (Nasdaq) market," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
Because it is ladened with technology stocks, the Nasdaq market took the brunt of Thursday's selloff in the high tech shares.

The Nasdaq composite posted its largest drop since July 23 on Thursday, tumbling 28 points, or two percent, to 1313. The selloff started in computer networking stocks following the proposed merger of 3Com Corp and U.S. Robotics Corp .
Stocks and bonds will be looking at the GDP data for confirmation that inflation pressures remain subdued, analysts said.

Regardless of the data, stocks are still saddled with caution brought on by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's warning on Wednesday that the market may have driven to unsustainable heights, said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities.
"We're in the throes of Alan Greenspan," he said. "I don't think numbers really count right now," he said.
Among special situations before the opening, Summit Bancorp and Collective Bancorp said they were merging. Cigna Corp said it was acquiring Healthsource Inc for $21.75 a share.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average fell 464.56 points, or 2.44 percent, to close at 18,557.00.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was off 38.0 at 4301.2.
U.S. shares traded in London were mixed in London.
The dollar was locked in a tight trading range in Europe, fighting to make headway against the yen and flat against the mark.
The 30-year U.S. Treasury was off 1/32 to yield 6.81. The Standard & Poors 500 futures index was flat at 792.50.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Greenspan appears to believe that investors are not concerned enough about the risks in the stock market. But some experts on Wall Street say Greenspan is worrying too much about the risks, it added.

The New York Times' Market Place column writes that 3Com's proposed takeover of U.S. Robotics got a skeptical reception on Thursday. The deal does not appear to give 3Com a large new advantage in its battle with leading computer networking company Cisco Systems Inc, the paper said, citing investors and industry analysts.
